headline: Medium risk: Chatwoot can expose customer data to Dagster workflows, but Dagster’s no-network/no-filesystem profile limits direct injection and conflict pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Chatwoot can surface messages and reports that may contain attacker-controlled text, while Dagster has no clipboard, stdin/stdout, MCP, or filesystem ingestion surfaces in its profile. That makes direct prompt injection into Dagster unlikely by default; the remaining pathway is unusual manual transfer or custom integration not shown here.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies Chatwoot message content into a Dagster task or prompt
IF a custom Dagster integration is added that ingests Chatwoot text without sanitization
mitigations: Sanitize Chatwoot text before any manual transfer
Use a fixed template for copied content
Disable ad hoc copy-paste into orchestration inputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to imported text

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, and messages, while Dagster is a data-engineering orchestrator. Even though Dagster has no network egress or filesystem read/write in the profile, the pair can still move sensitive Chatwoot data into pipeline metadata or logs if operators wire them together in default workflows.
conditions: IF Chatwoot customer records are passed into Dagster run metadata, logs, or asset materializations
IF a custom Dagster job serializes Chatwoot payloads into persistent storage
mitigations: Redact customer identifiers before orchestration
Keep Chatwoot payloads out of Dagster logs
Restrict pipeline inputs to non-sensitive aggregates
requires-engineering: add field-level allowlists
requires-engineering: configure retention limits for pipeline metadata

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Chatwoot has broad network egress, but Dagster’s profile explicitly disables filesystem write, modify_git_state, shell, subprocesses, and network egress. With no overlapping mutable write surface or shared OAuth scopes shown, a direct capability conflict is not plausible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF Dagster is reconfigured to gain write access to the same mutable resource as Chatwoot
IF both agents are later granted the same OAuth scope or shared database write path
mitigations: Keep Dagster read-only relative to Chatwoot outputs
Avoid shared mutable directories
Separate credentials per system
requires-engineering: add locking around any shared resource

D_cascading_error.rationale: Chatwoot can emit customer-support outputs that Dagster may consume in pipelines or metadata flows, so a mistaken Chatwoot result could cascade into downstream automation if treated as authoritative. Dagster’s profile does not show verification or human-review gates, so the safer assumption is that the pair can propagate errors unless explicitly checked.
conditions: IF Dagster jobs consume Chatwoot outputs without validation
IF Chatwoot-generated summaries are used as inputs to automated downstream actions
mitigations: Add a validation step before any Dagster action
Require human review for Chatwoot-derived inputs
Use schema checks on imported fields
Log source provenance for each downstream record

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot clearly handles customer data and messages, while Dagster is a general data-engineering system with no stated residency, retention, or certification controls in the profile. That creates a compliance mismatch risk if Chatwoot data is routed into Dagster logs or artifacts; the other agent is not cited for a specific residency violation because none is documented.
conditions: IF customer data from Chatwoot is stored in Dagster artifacts or logs
IF retention settings differ between Chatwoot records and Dagster metadata
mitigations: Minimize customer data sent to Dagster
Set short retention on pipeline logs
Document data-class handling rules
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows
requires-engineering: review residency and DPA obligations
